stages.title: Advanced grammar
stages.hook: Why do Portuguese speakers say 'Quero que você venha' and not 'Quero que você vem'?
explain: After verbs of wish, doubt, emotion and necessity Portuguese uses the subjunctive (subjuntivo in Brazil, conjuntivo in Portugal): 'Quero que você venha' (I want you to come), 'É importante que estudemos' (It is important that we study), 'Duvido que ele saiba' (I doubt he knows). The present subjunctive is formed from the eu form of the present: falo → fale, venho → venha.

Portuguese also has a personal infinitive, an infinitive with person endings: 'É importante estudarmos' (It is important for us to study), 'Para eles saírem' (for them to leave). Other advanced points: the imperfect subjunctive with the conditional ('Se eu tivesse tempo, viajaria': If I had time, I would travel), and the future subjunctive ('Quando você chegar, ligue').
stages.mnemonic: Want, doubt, hope: the next verb goes into the subjunctive.
items: It is important that we study
sentences: If I had time, I would travel.
It is important for us to study together.

gq.q: What is special about the personal infinitive?
o: It has no verb forms at all
It is used only for the past
It is a noun made from a verb
gq.why: It is a distinctive feature of Portuguese.

panel.q: How is the present subjunctive of 'falar' formed?
o: From the infinitive only: falar becomes fala
From eu falo: fale, fales, fale
By adding -ria to the stem: falaria
By adding -ndo to the stem: falando
panel.why: The eu stem plus the opposite vowel.

panel.q: Which sentence is a correct hypothetical?
Why 'Quando você chegar, ligue'?
o: Chegar is a noun, so the verb is in the imperative
It is a past event, so the verb is in the past
It is a question, so the verb is in the subjunctive
The future subjunctive follows quando in future time
panel.why: Quando plus future subjunctive for future time.

teach.model: Subjunctive follows wish, doubt, emotion and necessity. The personal infinitive has endings. Se + imperfect subjunctive + conditional makes hypothetical statements.

stages.title: Complex sentence patterns
stages.hook: How do you say 'the writer whose book I read'?
explain: Relative clauses: que (that, which, who) is the most common: 'O livro que li' (The book I read). 'Cujo' means 'whose' and agrees with the thing owned: 'O autor cujo livro li' (The author whose book I read), 'A escritora cuja obra admiro' (The writer whose work I admire). 'O qual / a qual' are used after prepositions in formal style: 'A casa na qual moro'.

The passive voice: ser + past participle: 'O livro foi escrito por Machado de Assis'. Also se passive: 'Vendem-se casas' (Houses are sold). Adverbial clauses: 'Embora chova, vou sair' (Although it rains, I will go out) with the subjunctive. Pronoun placement: Brazil prefers 'Me disse', Portugal 'Disse-me'; after não or que, pronouns go before the verb in both: 'Não me disse'.
stages.mnemonic: Cujo points to the owner and agrees with the owned thing.
items: the house in which I live
The book was written by him
O livro foi escrito por ele
sentences: The author whose book I read.
The book was written by Machado.
Although it rains, I will go out.

o: Ele escreve livros todos os dias
O livro foi escrito por ele

panel.q: Why is it 'cuja obra' and not 'cujo obra'?
o: Cujo is always masculine, in all forms
Obra is plural, so cujo changes
Cujo agrees with obra, which is feminine
Cuja is a verb meaning 'to belong'
panel.why: Cujo agrees with the thing owned.

panel.q: Why 'Não me disse' in both countries?
o: Brazil bans enclisis in all sentences
Portugal bans proclisis in all sentences
Disse is a noun here, not a verb
Negative words attract the pronoun before the verb
panel.why: After não the pronoun goes before the verb.

panel.q: Which clause needs the subjunctive?

teach.model: Que joins relative clauses; cujo means whose and agrees with the owned noun. Passive: ser + participle. Embora + subjunctive. Pronoun placement varies.

stages.title: Extended conversations
stages.hook: How do you keep a conversation going in Portuguese, using words like 'então' and 'pois'?
explain: Discourse markers keep conversations natural: 'Então' (so, then), 'Aliás' (by the way), 'Quer dizer' (I mean), 'Na verdade' (in fact), 'Sabe' (you know). In Brazil people often say 'Pois é' (that's true or well yes) and 'Né?' as a tag. In Portugal, 'Pois' alone often means 'Yes, indeed', and 'Pois é' too.

To agree: 'Concordo' (I agree), 'Com certeza' (certainly), 'Tem razão' (you are right). To disagree politely: 'Não concordo totalmente' (I do not completely agree), 'Por outro lado' (on the other hand). Ask for clarification: 'O que você quer dizer com isso?' Use active listening: 'Entendo', 'Sério?', 'Verdade?'
stages.mnemonic: Pois é, né, então: the glue of spoken Portuguese.
sentences: On the other hand, it is cheap.
What do you mean by that?

gq.why: It means that's right or indeed.

panel.q: Why use discourse markers?
o: They only add length to the sentences
They replace the verbs in a sentence
They are only decorative and can be left out
They make speech natural and organised

panel.q: Which phrase asks for clarification?
Which word signals an extra point?

teach.model: Use então, aliás, na verdade, quer dizer. Agree with concordo; disagree politely with não concordo totalmente. Ask O que você quer dizer?

points.ask: How do I ask for clarity?

stages.title: Formal and informal registers
stages.hook: When do you use 'tu', 'você' and 'o senhor' in Portuguese?
explain: Address forms depend on country and relationship. In Portugal, 'tu' is for friends, family and younger people; 'você' can sound distant or rude depending on context; and 'o senhor / a senhora' is polite for older people. In Brazil, 'você' is the usual 'you'; 'tu' is used in some regions such as the south and parts of the north-east; 'o senhor / a senhora' shows respect.

Formal letters: 'Prezado Senhor,' or 'Excelentíssimo Senhor' (Dear Sir), closing 'Atenciosamente' (Brazil) or 'Com os melhores cumprimentos' (Portugal). Informal: 'Oi, ...' and 'Abraço' or 'Beijinhos'. Use titles: Doutor/Doutora for professionals in Portugal. Match the register of the other person.
stages.mnemonic: Tu is close, você depends, o senhor is respect.
sentences: Dear Sir, thank you for your attention.
A hug and see you soon.

gq.q: Which closing is used in formal Brazilian letters?
Which pronoun is the everyday 'you' in most of Brazil?

panel.q: Why can 'você' be tricky in Portugal?
o: It may sound distant or inappropriate
It is always polite and formal
It is an old form no longer used
It is a plural form only
panel.why: Você can sound distant or even inappropriate in parts of Portugal, where tu or the senhor/senhora forms are preferred depending on the relationship.

panel.q: Which greeting is informal?
Why match register?
o: It is a rule of spelling in formal letters
It makes the text faster to read
It changes the meaning of the words

teach.model: Tu is informal in Portugal; você is standard in Brazil; o senhor/a senhora shows respect. Formal letters: Prezado Senhor, Atenciosamente (BR) or Com os melhores cumprimentos (PT).

stages.title: Reading articles and literature
stages.hook: Who wrote 'Os Lusíadas', 'Dom Casmurro' and 'A Hora da Estrela'?
explain: Famous works: Luís de Camões wrote the epic 'Os Lusíadas' (1572) about Portuguese explorers. Machado de Assis wrote 'Dom Casmurro' (1899), a Brazilian novel with an unreliable narrator. Eça de Queirós wrote 'Os Maias' (1888). Fernando Pessoa created several 'heteronyms'. Clarice Lispector wrote 'A Hora da Estrela' (1977), and Mia Couto (Mozambique) and Jorge Amado (Brazil) are other major authors.

When reading an article, find the main idea (ideia principal), supporting details (detalhes) and the writer's tone. In literature, ask about narrator, imagery, and historical context. Journalists use short sentences and reported speech: 'O ministro afirmou que ...' (The minister stated that ...), 'segundo o jornal ...' (according to the newspaper).
stages.mnemonic: Camões for the sea, Machado for doubt, Pessoa for many voices.
sentences: According to the newspaper, prices rose.
The article has a clear main idea.

o: era uma vez, the opening of tales
gq.why: It means according to the newspaper.

panel.q: What are Pessoa's heteronyms?
Why look for tone in an article?
o: It counts the words of the article
It shows the date of publication
It shows the font that was used

panel.q: What is the epic poem Os Lusíadas about?
o: A farm in the Brazilian interior
A school in a Portuguese village
panel.why: Os Lusíadas (1572), by Camões, celebrates the Portuguese voyages of discovery, above all Vasco da Gama's sea route to India.

teach.model: Find the main idea, supporting details and tone. Know major authors: Camões, Machado, Eça, Pessoa, Lispector, Couto.

stages.title: Essay and correspondence writing
stages.hook: How do you write a formal letter asking for information about a course?
explain: A formal letter or email has: greeting (Prezados Senhores,), purpose (Escrevo para solicitar informações sobre ...: I am writing to ask for information about ...), details, request (Agradeço desde já a atenção: Thank you in advance for your attention) and closing (Atenciosamente, + name).

For an essay: introdução (introduction), desenvolvimento (development) and conclusão (conclusion). Use connectors: 'Em primeiro lugar' (first of all), 'Além disso', 'No entanto' (however), 'Em conclusão' (in conclusion). Avoid slang and spoken shortenings such as pra and tá in formal writing. Check agreement, accents, and spelling variants: Brazil 'ação', Portugal formerly 'acção' (before the 1990 Orthographic Agreement came into force).
stages.mnemonic: Introdução, desenvolvimento, conclusão: a clear path.
items: I am writing to ask for
sentences: I am writing to ask for information.
Thank you in advance for your attention.
In conclusion, I agree with the idea.

gq.q: Which phrase opens a formal request?

panel.q: Why avoid slang in formal letters?
o: It is illegal in official letters
It is old and no longer understood
It makes the letter too long
panel.why: Slang clashes with the formal register readers expect in a letter to an institution.

panel.q: What order does an essay follow?
o: desenvolvimento only, without the other parts
introdução only, without the other parts
panel.why: Essays normally open with an introduction, develop arguments, and finish with a conclusion.

panel.q: What changed with the orthographic agreement?
o: The grammar of the language changed
The alphabet was replaced by another
The verbs were changed in all the countries

teach.model: Use Prezados Senhores, Escrevo para solicitar, Atenciosamente. Structure essays: introdução, desenvolvimento, conclusão. Use connectors.

points.ask: How do I frame a letter?
How do I structure an essay?

stages.title: Translation fundamentals
stages.hook: Why does 'pretender' not mean 'to pretend' in Portuguese?
explain: Translation requires attention to false friends. Portuguese 'pretender' means to intend; 'esquisito' means strange, not exquisite; 'atualmente' means currently, not actually; 'assistir' can mean to watch; 'parentes' are relatives, not parents (which are 'pais'); 'puxar' means to pull and 'empurrar' means to push; 'realizar' means to carry out.

Other points: Portuguese has gender for all nouns; English adjectives before nouns often move after; English phrasal verbs need a single Portuguese verb (give up = desistir). Translate meaning, not words. Always consider the variety: 'bus' is ônibus (Brazil) or autocarro (Portugal).
stages.mnemonic: Translate meaning; beware pretender, esquisito, parentes.
sentences: I intend to travel next year.

o: actually, in the sense of 'in fact'
finally, in the sense of 'at last'

panel.q: Why is 'esquisito' a false friend?
o: It is a verb meaning 'to exquisite'
It is a rude word in every country
It looks like exquisite but means strange
panel.why: Esquisito looks like English exquisite, but it means strange or odd.

panel.q: How do you translate 'give up'?
Why does the variety matter in translation?
o: Words differ in Brazil and Portugal
Verbs are lost in the other variety
panel.why: Words such as ônibus and autocarro differ between Brazil and Portugal, so the translator must know the audience.

teach.model: Beware false friends: pretender, esquisito, atualmente, parentes. Translate meaning, choose the correct variety.

stages.title: Regional varieties and cultural context
stages.hook: In which countries is Portuguese an official language, and does it sound the same everywhere?
explain: Portuguese is an official language in nine countries: Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cabo Verde, Guiné-Bissau, São Tomé e Príncipe, Timor-Leste and Equatorial Guinea. These countries form, with others, the CPLP (Community of Portuguese Language Countries), created in 1996. Macau also has Portuguese as an official language alongside Chinese.

Varieties: in Brazil, there are accents such as carioca (Rio), paulistano (São Paulo), nordestino (north-east) and gaúcho (south). In Portugal there are northern and southern accents, plus the Azores and Madeira. African varieties are influenced by local languages such as Kimbundu and Emakhuwa, and many people speak Portuguese as a second language. Creoles like Cape Verdean Creole are different languages.
stages.mnemonic: One language, many voices across four continents.
sentences: Portuguese is spoken on four continents.

gq.q: In which year was the CPLP created?
Which is a Brazilian regional accent?

panel.q: Why do African varieties differ?
o: Contact with local languages and second-language use
They are errors made by speakers
They are older than the European forms
They are written with another alphabet

panel.q: Is Cape Verdean Creole simply Portuguese?
o: Yes, exactly, with a few accents
No, it is a distinct creole
It is Spanish with Portuguese words
It is French with African words

panel.q: What is one benefit of a common standard?
o: It erases the accents of the regions
It stops the language from changing

teach.model: Portuguese is official in nine countries and in Macau, with many accents. CPLP unites Portuguese-speaking countries. Creoles are distinct languages.

stages.title: Structured debates and presentations
stages.hook: How do you structure a short talk and a debate turn in Portuguese?
explain: A presentation (apresentação) has an opening (Boa tarde a todos. Hoje vou falar sobre ...: Good afternoon everyone. Today I will talk about ...), development (Em primeiro lugar, em segundo lugar ...) and conclusion (Em resumo, ... Obrigado pela atenção). Use clear signposting and a steady pace.

In a debate: state your position (Defendo que ... : I argue that ...), give reasons (porque, uma vez que, dado que), address the other side (Entendo o seu ponto de vista, mas ...: I understand your view, but ...), and conclude. Phrases: 'Em minha opinião' (in my opinion), 'Na minha perspectiva', 'Gostaria de acrescentar' (I would like to add).
items: entendo seu ponto de vista, mas
sentences: Today I will talk about water.
I argue that education is essential.

o: Hoje vou falar sobre o tema
Defendo que a ideia é boa

panel.q: Why acknowledge the other side?
panel.why: Acknowledging the other side shows you have considered it and makes your argument more credible.

panel.q: Which connector gives a reason?
o: apesar de, which marks a concession

panel.q: What helps a clear talk?
o: Speed, so the talk finishes sooner
Long sentences, so the talk sounds serious
Slang only, so the talk sounds friendly

teach.model: Open with Hoje vou falar sobre..., signpost with em primeiro lugar, state a position with defendo que..., acknowledge with entendo seu ponto de vista, mas...

points.ask: How do I state a view?
How do I answer the other side?
